doc.title: David Torkanowsky interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, September 26, 2019

title: Who is responsible for time, the Sinatra big band, and goodbye
summary: Bass or drums for time: Neal swung a Sinatra centennial big band without the drummer; Mingus example; closing thanks.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: By the way I’m going to ask later, I’m going to ask Neal this question, I thought I’d ask you, in a piano trio who’s responsible — is any — is the bassist or the drummer more responsible for the time?

You would naturally probably tend to say the drummer but I’ll say this. I did a big band for the hundredth anniversary of Sinatra. And we got the original Nelson Riddle charts and Count Basie charts and Sammy Cahn? No. Another one of his bands. And we had Harry Shearer, we had a bunch of artists. And it was killer. Hand picked a big band, we rehearsed. And the drummer, I’m not going to say his name, cause he’s brilliant at everything and I’m surprised that he even played big band as well. I mean you could just Grady Tate it and you don’t have to [scats] you don’t have to do that, just swing. Anyway, this drummer missed the rehearsal due to a family illness and it was just Neal. Neal swung the fuck out of that band, just without a drummer. So I’m going to say probably both but the bassist, it depends on how assertive he is and how willing he is to agree or disagree. I mean if you listen to Mingus’s band, him and the drummer never really played time together but they agreed to disagree and it was still swinging. So again it’s that forward motion. It’s like we don’t have to get there in lock step but let’s go to the same place. So.
Well said. Okay. Thank you very much.
